The fertilised egg of Atlantic halibut (Hippoglossus hippoglossus) measures approximately 3 to 3.8 mm in diameter, and from this pelagic egg emerges a prolarva at eclosion with a total length of 0.65 cm , a value recorded from laboratory-reared clutches. After the hatching event, the yolk-sac larva continues its endotrophic development, relying exclusively on endogenous yolk reserves for nourishment. At a stable incubation temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C], the time from fertilisation to the hatching event is 18 days , a duration that is consistent with the slow developmental rates typical of cold-water marine teleosts. The prolarvae remain in the lecithotrophic stage, progressively absorbing their yolk mass, until the yolk-sac resorption is complete. The age at which this yolk absorption is completed, marking the end of the yolk-sac stage, is 50 days [ab = 50 days] under the same thermal regime, by which point the larva has reached a total length of 1.15 cm [Lb = 1.15 cm] at a temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C]. This prolonged reliance on maternal provisioning reflects the cold, low-metabolic environment of the species' early ontogeny.

Following the complete depletion of endogenous yolk stores, the exogenously feeding larva of Hippoglossus hippoglossus embarks on a pelagic larval phase that lasts several weeks. During this planktonic period, the larva grows steadily and attains a total length of 4 cm  by the time of larval metamorphosis, the point at which the dramatic allometric shift and body plan reorganisation associated with the larval-juvenile transition occur. The morphological transformation involves the migration of one eye to the opposite side of the head, a defining feature of flatfish. The initial wet weight at birth, measured shortly after the completion of yolk absorption, is 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams], a figure derived from the egg diameter and representing a modest starting mass. In contrast, the dry weight at birth, reflecting the purely structural organic content after desiccation, is substantially lower at 0.001476 grams , a value recorded after approximately 40 days of development at a slightly cooler temperature. This disparity between wet and dry mass underscores the high water content typical of marine fish larvae.

Sexual maturation in Atlantic halibut is a protracted process governed by water temperature, with most life-history milestones calibrated to the cold conditions of the North Atlantic. Under a background temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C], a regime that defines much of the species' energetic environment, females reach puberty at 2920 days since birth [tp = 2920 days since birth], a period equivalent to roughly eight years. Males, in contrast, mature faster, attaining sexual maturity at 2555 days since birth [tp = 2555 days since birth], or approximately seven years at a temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C]. This dimorphism in the pace of maturation is reflected in the size at which puberty is reached: females achieve a total length at puberty of 110 cm [Lp = 110 cm], while males mature at a substantially smaller body size, with a total length at puberty of 55 cm [Lp = 55 cm]. The difference likely reflects the greater energetic investment females must make in gamete production, necessitating a larger somatic frame before the onset of vitellogenesis. These values were compiled from field studies on commercial catches.

The ultimate body sizes attained by adult Hippoglossus hippoglossus exhibit pronounced sexual dimorphism, consistent with the patterns observed in many large-bodied flatfish. Females continue growing after reaching puberty and can ultimately achieve a total length of 350 cm [Li = 350 cm], a measurement that places them among the largest of the pleuronectiforms. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for females is 320,000 grams [Wwi = 320,000 grams], representing the maximum published weight for this sex. Males, by comparison, are considerably more modest in their final dimensions, reaching an ultimate total length of 180 cm [Li = 180 cm] and an ultimate wet weight of 83,000 grams [Wwi = 83,000 grams]. This disparity in maximum size has been linked to differential selective pressures, with larger females enjoying higher fecundity and thus transmitting more genes, while males may be constrained by the energetic costs of earlier maturation. The maximum lifespan for the species, under the same thermal conditions, extends to approximately 18,250 days [am = approximately 18,250 days], confirming a long-lived, slow-growing life history strategy at a temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C].

Reproductive output in female Atlantic halibut scales positively with body size, as field surveys of batch fecundity have demonstrated. A female of 132 cm total length produces approximately 470,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 470,000 eggs per spawning event], with a single spawning occurring annually [F_R_i = single spawning occurring annually], equivalent to a reproductive rate at TL 132 cm of approximately 1287.67 eggs per day  at a temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C]. At a larger body size of 195 cm total length, the same metric rises dramatically, with a female producing approximately 3,600,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 3,600,000 eggs per spawning event], also under an annual spawning frequency of one event per year [F_R_i = one event per year], all measured at a water temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C], corresponding to a reproductive rate at TL 195 cm of approximately 18273.97 eggs per day . These reproductive parameters underscore the species' strategy of investing in a few, highly fecund spawning events. Puberty, defined as the attainment of sexual maturity, occurs at 2920 days since birth [tp = 2920 days since birth] for females, marking the onset of reproductive capability at a temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C].
